title: Milk harvesting, parlour hygiene and equipment care processes on a dairy farm

lessons.title: Running a milking shift
lessons.html:
Your role in the parlour

In this work experience module you will work milking shifts in a real parlour under supervision, then take more responsibility as you become competent. Record each shift in your logbook: date, number of cows milked, problems seen and actions taken.

Before milking

  1. Check the parlour board for treated cows, mastitis cows and fresh cows.
  2. Check the plant was cleaned after the last milking and drained.
  3. Fit a new filter sock and check liners and tubes.
  4. Switch on, check the vacuum gauge reads correctly and pulsators are working.
  5. Prepare teat dips, towels, strip cup and gloves.
  6. Bring cows up quietly. Do not rush or shout.

During milking

  • Follow the farm's routine for every cow: fore-strip, pre-dip, contact time, dry, attach, adjust, remove, post-dip.
  • Work in a steady rhythm; on a herringbone, prepare a row while the other row milks.
  • Watch for kicking cows, falling clusters and cows that milk slowly.
  • Divert milk from treated, mastitis and colostrum cows away from the tank, using a separate bucket or dump line.
  • Hose dung off the platform as needed, keeping water away from udders being milked.

After milking

  • Check the bulk tank is cooling and record the temperature.
  • Look at the filter sock for clots or dirt and record what you see.
  • Start the wash cycle.
  • Clean the parlour floor, pit and yard.
  • Update the treatment and mastitis records.

Personal hygiene

Wear clean clothing, keep fingernails short, wear gloves, cover cuts and do not milk if you have a stomach illness. Do not smoke, eat or drink in the dairy.

lessons.title: Mastitis control in practice
lessons.html:
Mastitis: the costliest dairy disease

Mastitis is infection and inflammation of the udder. It reduces milk yield, raises somatic cell counts, leads to discarded milk and treatment costs, and can cause cows to be culled.

Two kinds

  • Clinical mastitis: you can see it. Clots, flakes, watery or bloody milk, a hot, hard or swollen quarter, sometimes a sick cow with fever.
  • Subclinical mastitis: the milk looks normal but the somatic cell count (SCC) is high. Found by milk recording or the California Mastitis Test (CMT).

Where infection comes from

SourceHow to prevent it
Other infected cows, via milkers' hands, towels and linersGloves, one towel per cow, post-dipping, milk infected cows last
The environment: dung, mud, wet beddingClean, dry lying areas and yards; pre-dipping; clean dry teats
Faulty equipmentCorrect vacuum, working pulsators, liners changed on time

Handling a clinical case

  1. Mark the cow and tell the supervisor.
  2. Milk her last or into a separate bucket.
  3. Treat according to the vet's protocol only.
  4. Record cow, quarter, date, treatment and withdrawal end date.
  5. Keep milk out of the tank until the withdrawal period on the label is over and the milk is normal.

Using CMT

Squirt milk from each quarter into the paddle cups, add the reagent, swirl and watch. A thick gel shows a high cell count. Record results and report positive quarters.

Cows keep standing after milking when they have fresh feed waiting, which gives the teat canal time to close before they lie down.

lessons.title: Cleaning and maintaining the plant
lessons.html:
Keeping the plant clean

You will carry out the farm's cleaning programme and keep its records.

Typical wash cycle

  1. Rinse milk out with lukewarm water, run to waste.
  2. Circulate hot alkaline detergent, at the temperature and strength on the label, for the set time. Check the return water is still hot at the end.
  3. Rinse.
  4. Acid wash as scheduled to remove milkstone.
  5. Sanitise before milking if the programme requires.

Signs of poor cleaning: white film or milkstone in the receiver jar, greasy feel inside liners, rising bacteria counts from the buyer.

Bulk tank

  • Record temperature after each milking and at collection.
  • Check the cooling compressor runs and the agitator turns.
  • Clean the tank after each collection, including the outlet valve and dipstick.

Maintenance schedule

  • Daily: vacuum level, pulsators, liners, hoses, filter.
  • Weekly: pump oil, belts, regulator cleaning.
  • Liners: replace after the number of milkings the maker states.
  • Professional plant test at the recommended interval.

Safety

  • Wear gloves, goggles and an apron when handling detergents and acids.
  • Never mix acid with chlorine products.
  • Add chemical to water, never water to chemical.
  • If chemical splashes in the eyes, rinse with running water for a long time and get medical help.
  • Switch off and isolate electrical equipment before maintenance; only qualified people do electrical work.
  • Keep floors clean to prevent slips.

Key points

  • Check the board, the plant and the vacuum before every milking.
  • Follow the full routine for every cow and keep abnormal milk out of the tank.
  • Prevent mastitis with hygiene, post-dipping and working equipment.
  • Clean the plant after every milking and record temperatures.
  • Handle cleaning chemicals with protective equipment and never mix acid and chlorine.
